basic_information.name: Strands Agents SDK
basic_information.creator: Amazon Web Services (AWS). Open-source community with contributions from Accenture, Anthropic, Langfuse, mem0.ai, Meta, PwC, Ragas.io, and Tavily.
basic_information.release_date: May 16-17, 2025 (initial open-source release under Apache 2.0). Strands Agents 1.0 announced July 2025 with production-ready multi-agent orchestration, A2A protocol support, and async improvements. Used internally at AWS (Amazon Q Developer, AWS Glue, VPC Reachability Analyzer) prior to public release.
basic_information.current_version: v1.25.0 (latest release on PyPI as of early 2026). The 1.0 milestone (July 2025) introduced multi-agent primitives and A2A support. TypeScript SDK also available (strands-agents/sdk-typescript). Tools package: strands-agents-tools v0.2.16+. Evals package: strands-agents-evals.

technical_architecture.architecture_pattern: single_agent | multi_agent | code_first — Strands uses a model-driven (model-first) architecture where the foundation model is the core of agent intelligence. The agent loop consults the LLM for what to do next rather than hardcoding a flow, relying on the model's reasoning to determine tool selection and sequencing. The core is a simple agentic loop connecting model + tools. Scales from single-agent conversational assistants to complex multi-agent orchestration. Multi-agent collaboration is modeled as tools — sub-agents are tools that the orchestrator agent can invoke, enabling hierarchical delegation.
technical_architecture.underlying_models: Model-agnostic via pluggable provider interface. Supported providers: (1) Amazon Bedrock — any model with tool use and streaming (Claude 4.5, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Claude 3 Opus/Haiku, Amazon Nova family, Llama, Mistral, Cohere, AI21). (2) Anthropic API directly — Claude model family. (3) Meta Llama via Llama API. (4) Ollama — local open-source models (Llama 3, Qwen3-VL, etc.) for edge and development. (5) OpenAI — GPT-4 and other models. (6) LiteLLM — access to 100+ additional providers through a universal adapter. Any model with reasoning and tool use capabilities can be used.
technical_architecture.tool_integration: Multi-layered tool system: (1) @tool decorator — any Python function becomes a tool by adding a simple decorator. (2) MCP (Model Context Protocol) — native support for thousands of published MCP servers, enabling instant connection to external services. (3) Community tools package (strands-agents-tools) — 20+ pre-built tools for file operations (read, write, edit), shell execution, HTTP requests, code interpretation, image generation, web search, memory (MongoDB, Elasticsearch), retrieval, and more. (4) Custom tool creation via Python functions. (5) Agents-as-tools — sub-agents exposed as tools for hierarchical orchestration. (6) MCP development server available in IDE for AI coding assistants.
technical_architecture.planning_approach: ReAct (model-driven) — The foundation model determines the sequence of steps autonomously. The agent loop iteratively: (1) sends context to the model, (2) the model reasons about what to do next, (3) selects and invokes appropriate tools, (4) processes results, (5) repeats until task completion. No hardcoded orchestration flow — the model figures out the optimal sequence. For multi-agent setups, the orchestrator model reasons about when to delegate to sub-agents. Supports both synchronous and asynchronous execution throughout the stack.
technical_architecture.multi_agent_support: First-class multi-agent support (GA in 1.0, July 2025) with four patterns: (1) Agents-as-Tools — hierarchical delegation where the orchestrator agent invokes specialized sub-agents as tools, mirroring how a project manager consults domain experts. (2) Handoffs — agents explicitly transfer control to other agents when their task is complete. (3) Swarm — agents autonomously determine when to hand off based on task completion, with shared state via invocation_state parameter. (4) Graph — structured workflows with conditional branches, where the LLM evaluates context and decides the best path forward; supports intelligent routing between agents. All patterns support shared state passing across agents. A2A (Agent-to-Agent) protocol support enables cross-platform agent communication.

memory_and_context.memory_types_supported: short_term | episodic | semantic — (1) Short-term: conversation history maintained within the agent's message list during a session. (2) Session management: persistent storage of conversation history and agent state across sessions, enabling continuity even after restarts or in distributed environments. (3) Long-term memory via AgentCore Memory: short-term memory stores raw conversation events within a session; long-term memory uses semantic extraction to persist facts across sessions. (4) Community tools for external memory backends: MongoDB memory, Elasticsearch memory. (5) Knowledge retrieval via RAG tools.
memory_and_context.context_window_management: Flexible ConversationManager interface with multiple strategies: (1) SlidingWindowConversationManager (default) — maintains a rolling window of recent messages, removing oldest messages when context limits are reached. (2) SummarizingConversationManager — intelligently summarizes older messages instead of discarding them, preserving important information while staying within context limits. Configurable parameters: summary_ratio (default 0.3, controls what percentage of messages to summarize), preserve_recent_messages (default 10, minimum recent messages to always keep). (3) Tool result truncation — configurable via should_truncate_results (default True); large tool results are truncated with placeholder messages when context is exceeded. (4) removed_message_count tracking for efficient session storage loading.
memory_and_context.persistence_mechanism: in_memory | database | cloud — (1) In-memory by default for development. (2) Session management enables persistence to remote datastores for production. (3) AgentCore Memory (managed AWS service) for short-term and long-term memory with semantic extraction. (4) Community memory backends: MongoDB, Elasticsearch. (5) Custom session managers can persist to any storage backend.
memory_and_context.context_engineering_approach: Context is managed as a first-class concern through the ConversationManager interface. Developers can choose and configure context management strategies (sliding window, summarization, or custom). The model-driven approach means context is the primary input to the LLM for reasoning — what goes into context directly determines agent behavior. Shared state across multi-agent systems via invocation_state parameter enables context sharing without exposing it to the LLM. Session management provides cross-session context continuity. AgentCore Memory adds semantic extraction for persistent knowledge. The system separates conversation context (messages) from shared state (invocation_state) from persistent memory (sessions/AgentCore).

capabilities.core_capabilities: Comprehensive open-source agent framework with: (1) Model-driven agent loop — simple yet powerful core connecting model + tools, where the LLM drives all planning and execution decisions. (2) Minimal code to get started — functional agent in 3-4 lines of Python code. (3) Multi-agent orchestration — four patterns (Agents-as-Tools, Handoffs, Swarm, Graph) for complex collaboration. (4) Native MCP support — connect to thousands of published MCP servers for instant tool access. (5) 20+ community-built tools — file operations, shell, HTTP, code interpreter, image generation, web search, memory systems, retrieval. (6) @tool decorator — turn any Python function into an agent tool with one line. (7) Pluggable model providers — switch between Bedrock, Anthropic, OpenAI, Ollama, LiteLLM with a config change. (8) Conversation management — sliding window and summarization strategies for context optimization. (9) Session management — persist and restore agent state across interactions. (10) Full async support — non-blocking concurrent execution throughout the stack. (11) Built-in observability — OpenTelemetry instrumentation, tracing, logging, and metrics out of the box. (12) Agent SOPs — natural language standard operating procedures that define structured workflows. (13) Streaming support — real-time response streaming. (14) Evaluation SDK (strands-agents-evals) for agent quality assessment. (15) Deploy anywhere — local, Lambda, Fargate, EKS, EC2, or Bedrock AgentCore.
capabilities.supported_modalities: Text, code (code interpreter tool, shell execution), file system (read, write, edit tools), HTTP/API calls, web search, image generation (via Nova Reels/image tools), vision (via multimodal models like Qwen3-VL on Ollama or Claude on Bedrock), browser interaction (via AgentCore Browser tool).
capabilities.autonomy_level: fully_autonomous | human_in_loop — Configurable. By default, agents operate autonomously within their defined tool set. Human-in-the-loop can be implemented through custom tools that pause for approval, or via application-layer integration. AgentCore deployment adds guardrails for content filtering. The model-driven approach means the LLM decides tool usage autonomously unless constrained.
capabilities.tool_ecosystem: Extensive and growing: (1) strands-agents-tools package with 20+ pre-built tools across categories: file operations (file_read, file_write, file_edit), system (shell, environment), network (http_request), code (code_interpreter), search and retrieval (retrieve, web search), media (generate_image, nova_reels), memory (mongodb_memory, elasticsearch_memory), agent orchestration. (2) MCP ecosystem — thousands of published MCP servers for external service integration. (3) AgentCore tools — Code Interpreter (sandboxed Python/JS/TS execution), Browser (web interaction). (4) Custom tools via @tool decorator. (5) Agents-as-tools for hierarchical delegation.

agent_interoperability.mcp_support: Yes — native, first-class MCP support. Strands agents can connect to any published MCP server, providing access to thousands of ready-made tools. The SDK includes an MCP client for connecting to MCP servers. An MCP development server is also available for IDE integration, giving AI coding assistants access to Strands documentation and development prompts.
agent_interoperability.a2a_support: Yes — A2A (Agent-to-Agent) protocol support was added in Strands 1.0 (July 2025). The A2A protocol, originally developed by Google and transitioning to the Linux Foundation for open governance, enables cross-platform agent communication. Strands agents can act as both A2A clients and servers, enabling interoperability with agents built on different frameworks.
agent_interoperability.agents_md_support: No native AGENTS.md support documented. Strands Agents uses its own Agent SOPs (Standard Operating Procedures) system for defining structured workflows in natural language. Agent SOPs are compatible with Anthropic's Claude Skills format. Agent instructions are provided via the system prompt parameter when creating an agent.
agent_interoperability.cross_framework_compatibility: Strong — (1) Strands is framework-agnostic and can coexist with other frameworks. (2) When deployed on AgentCore Runtime, it runs alongside agents built with LangChain, LangGraph, CrewAI, and LlamaIndex. (3) MCP support enables standardized tool sharing with any MCP-compatible framework. (4) A2A protocol enables cross-framework agent communication. (5) LiteLLM integration provides model access across 100+ providers. (6) OpenTelemetry observability integrates with any OTEL-compatible monitoring stack. (7) Can be combined with LangGraph in the same multi-agent system (agents-as-tools pattern allows wrapping other frameworks' agents).

safety_and_guardrails.permission_model: capability_based | sandbox — (1) Tool-level permissions: agents can only use tools explicitly provided to them via the tools parameter. (2) @tool decorator defines tool boundaries. (3) Shell and file tools can be configured for specific paths/commands. (4) When deployed on AgentCore: Bedrock Guardrails for content filtering, PII protection, and topic blocking. (5) AgentCore Policy (preview) for fine-grained Cedar-based permissions on tool calls. (6) IAM-based access control for AWS resources. (7) Code Interpreter runs in sandboxed environments. (8) VPC isolation available for network-level security.
safety_and_guardrails.escalation_policy: Application-layer implementation. The framework does not enforce a built-in escalation path, but supports it through: (1) Custom tools that pause execution and request human input. (2) Multi-agent supervisor patterns where sub-agents can escalate to the orchestrator. (3) When deployed on AgentCore: Guardrails can block or flag responses, AgentCore Policy can restrict tool access requiring approval. (4) Developers implement escalation logic in tool functions or application code.
safety_and_guardrails.hallucination_mitigation: Multi-strategy: (1) Model-driven grounding — the LLM's own reasoning capabilities ground responses in tool outputs. (2) RAG via retrieval tools grounds responses in enterprise documents. (3) When deployed on AgentCore: Bedrock Guardrails with Automated Reasoning checks use formal logic to verify AI-generated information with up to 99% accuracy. (4) Contextual grounding checks verify responses against provided context. (5) Tool results provide deterministic data that anchors agent responses. (6) Evaluation SDK (strands-agents-evals) monitors correctness and quality. (7) Full tracing enables post-hoc verification of agent reasoning chains.
safety_and_guardrails.audit_trail: Yes — built-in via OpenTelemetry instrumentation. Every agent execution produces traces with spans showing model calls, tool invocations, reasoning steps, and execution times. Traces exportable to Jaeger, Grafana Tempo, AWS X-Ray, Datadog, and other OTEL-compatible backends. When on AgentCore: CloudWatch stores all metrics and traces, CloudTrail logs API calls.
safety_and_guardrails.human_oversight_pattern: pre-approval | post-review — (1) Pre-approval: implement custom tools that pause for human input before critical actions. (2) Post-review: full tracing and logging enable review of all agent actions. (3) Guardrails (on AgentCore) screen inputs and outputs. (4) Evaluation SDK provides continuous quality monitoring. (5) Multi-agent supervisor patterns enable oversight of sub-agent actions. (6) No built-in confidence-threshold mechanism — developers implement this in custom logic.

governance_and_standards.governance_body: Amazon Web Services governs the open-source project under Apache 2.0 license. Community contributions from Accenture, Anthropic, Meta, PwC, Langfuse, mem0.ai, Ragas.io, and Tavily. GitHub organization: github.com/strands-agents. The A2A protocol (supported by Strands) is transitioning to the Linux Foundation for open governance.
governance_and_standards.contributing_protocols: Implements MCP (Model Context Protocol) by Anthropic for tool integration. Supports A2A (Agent-to-Agent) protocol by Google/Linux Foundation for cross-platform agent communication. Uses OpenTelemetry (OTEL) for observability and distributed tracing. Exports to AWS X-Ray format and W3C trace formats. Agent SOPs compatible with Anthropic's Claude Skills format.
governance_and_standards.regulatory_compliance: Strands Agents SDK itself has no regulatory certifications (it is a developer library). However, when deployed on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, it inherits AWS compliance certifications: SOC 1/2/3, HIPAA (with BAA), GDPR, ISO 27001, and others. Enterprises can use IAM, VPC, KMS encryption, and PrivateLink for data sovereignty. No specific EU AI Act compliance statement, though the tracing and audit capabilities support required traceability. Local deployment with Ollama enables full data sovereignty. [uncertain]

deployment_and_operations.deployment_modes: local | cloud | hybrid | edge | managed_service — (1) Local: run agents on any machine with Python and Ollama for development or edge deployment. (2) AWS Lambda: serverless deployment for short-lived agent interactions. (3) AWS Fargate / Amazon EKS: containerized deployment with streaming support for interactive applications. (4) Amazon EC2: maximum control for high-volume or specialized requirements. (5) Amazon Bedrock AgentCore: fully managed serverless runtime with auto-scaling, identity, memory, and observability built in. (6) Edge: Ollama provider enables running on edge devices with local open-source models. (7) Any Python environment: standard pip install, no AWS dependency required for basic usage.
deployment_and_operations.scalability_model: serverless | horizontal — On AgentCore Runtime: fully managed auto-scaling with consumption-based billing (idle time and I/O wait are free). On Lambda: serverless scaling. On Fargate/EKS: horizontal container scaling. Configurable max_parallel_tools parameter to limit concurrent tool execution based on infrastructure capacity. Async support throughout the stack enables true concurrent execution.
deployment_and_operations.cost_per_task: The SDK itself is free and open-source. Costs come from model inference and infrastructure: (1) Model inference: varies by provider — Amazon Bedrock token pricing, Anthropic API pricing, OpenAI pricing, or free with local Ollama models. (2) AgentCore Runtime: consumption-based pricing (CPU + memory per second, I/O wait is free — saving 30-70% vs. traditional compute since agents spend most time waiting for LLM responses). (3) Lambda: standard AWS Lambda pricing. (4) A simple agent task with Claude on Bedrock might cost $0.01-$0.10; complex multi-agent workflows could be $0.50-$5.00+ depending on model and tool calls. (5) Local deployment with Ollama: zero API cost (hardware only).
deployment_and_operations.resource_requirements: Minimal for development: Python 3.10+, pip install strands-agents. No GPU required (LLM inference runs on provider infrastructure or local CPU/GPU via Ollama). Standard development machine sufficient. Optional: Docker/Finch/Podman for containerized testing. For production: depends on deployment target — Lambda requires AWS account; AgentCore requires Bedrock access; self-hosted requires appropriate compute for expected load. Edge deployment: device capable of running Ollama with chosen model.

observability_and_ops.monitoring_integration: Built-in OpenTelemetry (OTEL) instrumentation providing telemetry collection, logging, and metrics out of the box. Compatible backends: (1) AWS X-Ray (native). (2) Amazon CloudWatch (native on AgentCore). (3) Jaeger. (4) Grafana Tempo. (5) Datadog. (6) Langfuse (community integration, Langfuse is a contributing partner). (7) Any OTEL-compatible monitoring backend. AgentCore Observability dashboard provides pre-built visualizations for trace analysis, error breakdowns, and performance metrics.
observability_and_ops.tracing_support: Yes — comprehensive, built-in from day one. Every agent execution produces OpenTelemetry traces with spans for each operation: model calls, tool invocations, reasoning steps, and multi-agent coordination. Traces include operation names, start/end times, attributes, and hierarchical span relationships. Exportable to any OTEL-compatible backend. Supports AWS X-Ray format and W3C trace formats.
observability_and_ops.production_readiness_level: production_ready — Used in production at AWS teams (Amazon Q Developer, AWS Glue, VPC Reachability Analyzer) before public release. Version 1.0 (July 2025) explicitly marketed as production-ready. Over 1M downloads and 150K+ PyPI downloads by preview period. Backed by AWS engineering. However, as an open-source SDK (not a managed service), production readiness depends on the deployment infrastructure chosen. On AgentCore: enterprise_grade. Self-hosted: production_ready with appropriate DevOps.

adoption_and_market.github_stars: ~5,065 stars on strands-agents/sdk-python (as of February 2026). Over 2,000 stars achieved within weeks of the May 2025 launch. The strands-agents GitHub organization hosts multiple repos: sdk-python, sdk-typescript, tools, docs, samples, agent-builder. Also forked/mirrored by Stability AI.
adoption_and_market.adoption_scale: 1M+ downloads by September 2025. 150K+ PyPI downloads during the preview period (May-July 2025). Used in production by AWS internal teams: Amazon Q Developer, AWS Glue, VPC Reachability Analyzer — where it reduced agent development from months to days/weeks. Community: 80% of 600 agents in AWS AI hackathon built using Strands. Growing partner ecosystem: Accenture, Anthropic, Meta, PwC, Langfuse, mem0.ai, Ragas.io, Tavily. Multiple AWS blog posts, tutorials, and courses published. TypeScript SDK also available.
adoption_and_market.pricing_model: open-source (free) — The SDK itself is completely free under Apache 2.0. Costs arise only from chosen model providers (Bedrock, Anthropic, OpenAI, etc.) and deployment infrastructure (AWS services, self-hosted). No per-agent or per-action fees from Strands itself. Zero cost possible with local Ollama deployment.
adoption_and_market.key_use_cases: Developer tooling (Amazon Q Developer — coding assistant), data engineering (AWS Glue — automated ETL), network analysis (VPC Reachability Analyzer), enterprise automation, customer service agents, education (LibreChat integration for educational institutions), cloud infrastructure management (AWS Cloud Engineer agent), research agents, multi-agent collaboration workflows, physical AI (edge deployment with NVIDIA GR00T and Hugging Face LeRobot), content generation.
adoption_and_market.competitive_position: Strong and rapidly growing open-source alternative to LangChain/LangGraph, CrewAI, and AutoGen. Key differentiators: (1) Model-first philosophy — minimal code, the LLM drives orchestration vs. developer-coded graphs/flows. (2) Native MCP support — access to thousands of tools instantly vs. custom integrations. (3) AWS ecosystem integration — seamless deployment to AgentCore, Lambda, Fargate for AWS-centric teams. (4) Production-proven — used in major AWS services before public release, unlike many academic or startup frameworks. (5) Backed by AWS engineering and enterprise resources. Weaknesses: (1) Newer than LangChain/LangGraph (less community content and third-party tooling). (2) Perception of AWS vendor lock-in (though the SDK itself is cloud-agnostic). (3) Less visual/no-code tooling compared to some competitors. Compared to LangGraph: simpler API, less granular control over execution graphs. Compared to CrewAI: less opinionated about agent roles/personas, more flexible.

human_agent_interaction.autonomy_spectrum: autonomous | assistant — Default is autonomous: the agent reasons and acts independently within its tool set. Can be configured as assistant mode by implementing tools that request human approval for actions. Multi-agent supervisor patterns add hierarchical oversight. The model-driven approach means the LLM decides what to do, not the developer's code.
human_agent_interaction.handoff_mechanism: Multi-agent patterns provide structured handoff: (1) Handoffs pattern — agents explicitly transfer control to other agents. (2) Swarm pattern — agents autonomously determine when to hand off based on task completion. (3) Agents-as-Tools — orchestrator delegates to specialized sub-agents and receives results back. (4) Human handoff implemented at the application layer through custom tools that pause execution for human input. No built-in human escalation UI — handoff is implemented via tool functions or application integration.
human_agent_interaction.feedback_loop: Evaluation SDK (strands-agents-evals) enables automated quality assessment using RAGAS metrics and custom evaluators. Langfuse integration provides tracing and analytics for identifying improvement areas. AgentCore Memory enables agents to accumulate knowledge from past interactions. No built-in explicit thumbs-up/thumbs-down feedback mechanism — improvement relies on evaluation metrics, prompt engineering, tool refinement, and memory accumulation. Developers can build custom feedback tools.

entrepreneurial_relevance.startup_applicability: Strands Agents is an excellent choice for startups building AI agent products, especially those considering AWS infrastructure. Best for: (1) Teams wanting to prototype fast — a functional agent in 3-4 lines of Python, with production deployment path clear from day one. (2) AWS-invested startups — seamless path from local development to Lambda/AgentCore production. (3) Teams needing model flexibility — switch between Claude, GPT-4, Llama, or local models without code changes. (4) Startups building multi-agent systems — four built-in orchestration patterns save months of development vs. rolling your own. (5) Cost-conscious teams — run locally with Ollama (free), then scale to cloud when needed. (6) Teams requiring enterprise credibility — 'built on AWS technology used in Amazon Q Developer' is a strong sales narrative. When to avoid: (1) If you need maximum community ecosystem and third-party tooling today — LangChain/LangGraph has more community content. (2) If you want role-based agent personas out of the box — CrewAI's crew/agent metaphor may be more intuitive. (3) If you need visual/no-code agent design — look at Google ADK or Vertex AI Agent Builder. (4) If you prefer maximum control over execution graphs — LangGraph offers more granular flow control.
entrepreneurial_relevance.build_vs_buy: Use Strands (open-source, free) when: you want full control over your agent architecture, you need model-provider flexibility, you're building for production and want a proven framework, or you want to avoid per-agent/per-action platform fees. Combine with AgentCore (managed service, paid) when: you need managed memory, identity, and observability without building infrastructure, you need enterprise compliance (SOC2, HIPAA), or you want auto-scaling without DevOps. The Strands + AgentCore combination offers the best of both worlds for AWS-centric startups: open-source flexibility during development, enterprise infrastructure for production. Compared to CrewAI Enterprise: Strands is fully open-source with no proprietary tier. Compared to LangChain: Strands is simpler but less mature ecosystem. For early-stage startups, Strands' zero-cost local development + pay-as-you-go cloud deployment is ideal.

confidence.cross_reference: AWS Open Source Blog (introduction May 2025, 1.0 announcement July 2025), AWS Machine Learning Blog (technical deep dive, multi-agent patterns), strandsagents.com official documentation, GitHub strands-agents/sdk-python, PyPI strands-agents package, AWS Prescriptive Guidance framework comparison, InfoQ coverage, SiliconANGLE coverage, MarkTechPost coverage, Langfuse blog comparison of agent frameworks, SelectHub LangChain vs Strands comparison, Medium technical analyses, DEV Community tutorials.
confidence.caveats: The framework is young (public since May 2025, 1.0 since July 2025) and evolving rapidly — API and features may change. GitHub stars (~5,065) based on Bedrock Agents research cross-reference (February 2026) but may have grown since. The TypeScript SDK is newer and less mature than the Python SDK. While the SDK is cloud-agnostic, the strongest deployment path is AWS, creating a soft vendor preference. Community ecosystem is smaller than LangChain/LangGraph but growing fast. Some advanced features (Guardrails, Policy, Evaluations) require AgentCore managed service rather than the open-source SDK alone. Production readiness claims are backed by internal AWS usage but public production case studies outside AWS are limited. Regulatory compliance applies only when deployed on AgentCore/AWS, not to the open-source SDK itself.
